title: The turban in the code
hookLine: the code asks men to wear a turban; women may choose to

lines: A STRIP OF CLOTH, A MIRROR.
cards: Early morning, in front of a mirror. A long strip of cloth, starched or soft, is shaken out and folded lengthwise. One end goes between the teeth to hold it.
Then the wrapping starts: around, up, across, pleat by pleat, each layer laid flat over the last, the hands moving the way hands move after years of the same thing. A pin tucked here.
A last pass at the front, checked in the mirror, nudged a finger's width. Done. It took a few minutes, and the whole day will be lived inside it.

teach.h: THE CODE: MEN WEAR IT; WOMEN MAY.
teach.b: Way back on day three, you met the turban as a crown you tie yourself. Today, the code. Dastar is the Sikh turban.

The Sikh Rehat Maryada says, in paraphrase, that a Sikh man must wear a turban, and that for a Sikh woman it's optional. Some Sikh women tie a dastar every day; others cover their hair with a long scarf, a chunni.
Both are within the code. Why a turban at all? It starts with the hair.
Keeping the hair uncut, kesh, is part of the Sikh way, and the code asks Sikhs to keep it.

teach.h: IT COVERS AND KEEPS THE KESH.
teach.b: A turban covers it, keeps it clean and tidy, and keeps the comb, the kangha, tucked inside. So the dastar isn't decoration on top of the faith; it's how the uncut hair, kept as a gift, is cared for. Then what it says.
Sikhs speak of the dastar as a crown, given by the Guru. Tradition says that in the Gurus' world a turban could mark rank and nobility.
On a Sikh head it's worn by a farmer, a teacher and a surgeon alike; nobody's turban is a lower one.
And a crown carries weight. A Sikh in a turban can't blend into a crowd; a stranger may remember what they do as what a Sikh did.
Some Sikhs call that the turban's quiet job: a daily reminder to act like someone the Guru crowned. That's why, for Sikhs who wear it, being told to remove it is no small thing. It isn't a hat.
It's part of the self, tied fresh each morning.

how: Sikh men tie a dastar to cover their uncut hair, often freshly each morning; Sikh women may wear one too or cover their hair with a chunni, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada leaves the turban optional for women.

practice: Take any cloth near you, a scarf, a towel, a napkin, shake it out, and fold it slowly, edge to edge, smoothing each fold flat with your palm before the next.
Then rest your hands on it in your lap and breathe, noticing how something ordinary now looks cared for.

wordCard.voice: Dastar. The Sikh turban: required by the code for men, a choice for women, covering the uncut hair and worn as a crown from the Guru. Today's word.
